PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bus Stop — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole first bus ride — waiting, boarding, riding and ringing — before the real one happens.

What is this?

A bus stop is a little shelter with a bench and a sign, where the bus arrives on a schedule to carry everyone along its route.

What does it mean?

Shared rides are the idea: one big bus, one driver, and a whole street of people going the same way — the town&rsquo;s moving meeting room.

What does the child need to know?

You need the timetable (when does the bus come?), a fare or a tap-card, and the patience of the bench — the bus runs on its own clock, not ours.

Why this matters

Not everyone has a car, and even cars stay home sometimes — the bus carries the whole town: to school, to work, to the pool, and home again.

What it teaches

Waiting for a schedule, boarding in turn, sitting while riding, and the stop-button decision — timing a press is real planning for small hands.

Words to learn

bus stopbusshelterbenchtimetabledriverfaretapstop buttonroute

Say this to your child

“"The bus stop! Bench, timetable, watch the street... HERE IT COMES! Wave! Tap — beep! Find a seat. The town rolls past the window — look, the bakery! Bing! Our stop! Step down — bus ride complete!"”

Step by step

  1. Check the timetable — the bus comes at its own time, and the timetable knows it.
  2. Wait on the bench and watch down the street — a big shape with lights is getting closer...
  3. Wave! Board in turn and tap the card — beep! — then find a seat or hold the pole like a sailor.
  4. Watch the windows: the town scrolls by — the bakery! the library! — count the stops.
  5. Press the stop button a little early — bing! — the driver nods, the bus slows, and off you step, right where you planned.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the shelter stands with a big round bus sign and a bench inside — the smallest building in town, and one of the busiest.

Ask your child

"What do we do while we wait?" (sit on the bench, watch for the bus) "What do we tap when we get on?" (our card — beep!) "When do we press the button?" (a little before our stop — bing!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run a full bus route through the house with cushion stops, ring an invisible bell for the refrigerator stop, or wave at real buses with such commitment that drivers wave back (they always do).

Out in the real world

Waiting in line is a queue in the UK and a line in the US and Canada — both start at a bus stop. Practicing the bench-wave-tap-sit routine at home makes the first real ride smooth, and the stop button becomes a trusted friend.

Try it together

Bus route around the house: chairs in a line, tickets torn from paper, stops called at the fridge (Stop 1: Kitchen), the bookshelf (Stop 2: Library) and the bathroom (Stop 3: Splash Pools). Driver rotates every lap — bing!

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do at the shelter?" (wait for the bus) "What do we press before our stop?" (the button — bing!)

This lesson pairs with the Bus Stop flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.
